evidence.claim: A $10M ARR B2B SaaS finance team had inconsistent figures across billing, accounting, and CRM systems, creating a recurring investor-reporting problem.
evidence.quote: A B2B SaaS company at $10M ARR had outgrown their reporting infrastructure. Revenue data lived in Stripe, accounting data in QuickBooks Online, and customer data in HubSpot. None of these systems agreed with each other. The VP of Finance was maintaining 12 separate Excel workbooks to reconcile the three systems and produce investor-grade metrics. Every month was a fire drill—and trust in the numbers was eroding.

evidence.claim: The existing workaround consumed substantial finance time and delayed board and diligence reporting.
evidence.quote:
- 12 Excel workbooks required to reconcile Stripe → QBO and produce investor metrics
- 20+ hours per month spent on manual data reconciliation and report assembly
- No real-time visibility into MRR, churn, expansion, or contraction
- Revenue recognition done manually — annual contracts recognized as monthly Stripe charges hit, not on an accrual basis
- Board meeting prep started on day 1 after close and still wasn't ready by day 10
- Investor due diligence requests took days to fulfill because data wasn't centralized

evidence.claim: A separate SaaS case study corroborates manual reconciliation of MRR and churn across systems for every board or investor report.
evidence.quote: Revenue reporting was spread across CSV exports, manual spreadsheet joins, and dashboard logic baked directly into the BI layer. Every new board or investor report meant someone manually reconciling MRR and churn numbers across systems, and nobody could say with confidence why two reports sometimes told different stories.

evidence.claim: A governed custom data layer and BI dashboard are a demonstrated alternative to purchasing a packaged subscription-analytics product.
evidence.quote: Consolidated CRM, billing, and finance data into a single governed data layer, replacing manual exports. Rebuilt core revenue metrics, including MRR, churn, and expansion, as documented, version-controlled logic instead of one-off spreadsheet formulas. Delivered a single RevOps reporting dashboard that gave the whole team one trusted number from source systems to board pack.

evidence.claim: Some finance teams in this audience require accounting functions beyond subscription analytics, creating a material product-boundary risk.
evidence.quote:
### Revenue Recognition Engine

- • **Subscription classification:** Each Stripe subscription automatically classified as monthly, annual, or multi-year with appropriate recognition schedule
- • **Deferred revenue tracking:** Annual payments automatically spread over the contract period. Deferred revenue balance calculated daily.
- • **Revenue waterfall:** MRR decomposed into new, expansion, contraction, churn, and reactivation — automatically, from Stripe event data
- • **Stripe → QBO reconciliation:** Automated matching of Stripe charges to QBO invoices/payments with exception reporting for mismatches
evidence.impact_reason: The documented solution includes accrual schedules, deferred revenue, and accounting-system reconciliation. None is established by the supplied ChartMogul product truth, so buyers requiring the complete finance workflow may still need a separate governed data and accounting layer.

segments.who: Recurring-revenue SaaS companies where finance or RevOps must reconcile operational subscription metrics for executives, investors, or diligence.
segments.why_them: Two independent public case studies show the same observable workflow: billing, CRM, and finance figures disagree, spreadsheets proliferate, and board reporting becomes a recurring reconciliation exercise. ChartMogul plausibly replaces part of this workflow by normalizing subscription data, but accounting-grade reporting remains a separate requirement.
segments.trigger: Upcoming board meeting, financing round, diligence request, recent finance hire, multiple revenue systems, or repeated disagreement over ARR and MRR.
pains: Different systems produce different MRR or ARR figures.
Board-pack preparation consumes days of manual exports and reconciliation.
Metric definitions are difficult to trace and defend during investor questions.
Subscription edge cases introduce quiet inconsistencies into spreadsheet models.
segments.objection: ChartMogul reports subscription-management metrics, not necessarily GAAP revenue recognition, accounting close, or the complete governed data model required by larger finance teams. Support for specific accounting integrations is unresolved from the supplied capability catalogue. Price-sensitive operators may prefer Stripe, spreadsheets, or a custom BI layer.
segments.angle: Replace the recurring pre-board reconciliation exercise with a normalized subscription model whose movements can be traced to customers and segments.
segments.basis: Independent consulting case studies document this workflow at growth-stage B2B SaaS companies, while ChartMogul's customer directory names matching fundraising and custom-contract situations. The supplied product brief establishes ChartMogul as the product owner and identifies subscription analytics as its category. Core MRR, ARR, churn, and retention calculation is stated in the product brief but has no supplied capability ID, so it is not encoded as a required capability. Accounting-grade revenue recognition, audit controls, and native accounting-system support remain unknown and should be qualified before outreach.
